name: Galvanize-Null
geological_features: Impact-scarred wastelands covering the entire surface
Solar wind erosion patterns etched into bare rock
Galvanized mineral coating on sun-facing surfaces
description: Galvanize-Null is a small, airless rock hammered by impacts and baked by unfiltered radiation until its sun-facing surfaces have developed a thin metallic coating deposited by solar wind, giving them a galvanized appearance that gleams against the otherwise dead grey terrain. The impact cratering is severe, with craters overlapping craters in a geological record of bombardment stretching back to the system's formation. Without atmosphere, the surface transitions from blistering heat in sunlight to extreme cold in shadow with knife-edge precision.

The world radiates nullity, an absence of anything that might make it remarkable save for the galvanized sheen on its sunward face. The silence is complete, the landscape is monochromatic grey broken only by the metallic gleam of the solar deposits, and the only movement is the slow crawl of the terminator line as the planet rotates. Standing on the surface, the universe feels close and indifferent, the stars bright and sharp overhead, the ground dead beneath one's feet.

A collection of defunct satellites from various eras orbits the planet in slowly decaying trajectories, creating a sparse satellite graveyard that tells the story of successive survey missions, each apparently concluding that the world held nothing of interest. The satellites date from at least four different civilizations, spanning thousands of years, suggesting that Galvanize-Null has been checked and dismissed repeatedly by an interstellar community that found it wanting. The only anomaly is that so many civilizations bothered to survey it at all.

The planet's mineral resources are common and accessible but not exceptional enough to justify dedicated mining operations when asteroids offer similar materials with less gravitational cost. The satellite graveyard has minor salvage value, and the oldest satellites may have archaeological significance. Galvanize-Null's only real utility is as a navigation landmark, its galvanized face visible in the infrared from considerable distance, and some charts already mark it as a waypoint for travelers passing through this otherwise unremarkable system.
